hops.title: Turn the walk to your bed into a memory palace
hops.text: Picture a pineapple, yellow rubber boots, toothpaste, a violin and a brick, each set at a spot on the walk from your door to your bed. This is the method of loci. Brain scans and cognitive tests of World Memory Championship competitors found brain structure and general intelligence comparable to controls. What stood out was strategy: most used a mental route, and navigation areas including the hippocampus were more active as they memorized. Beginners who trained in the method for six weeks shifted their resting brain connectivity toward the champions' pattern and recalled more of a 72-word list than controls, an edge still there when retested four months later.

sources.citation: Maguire, E. A., Valentine, E. R., Wilding, J. M., & Kapur, N. (2003). Routes to remembering: the brains behind superior memory. Nature Neuroscience, 6(1), 90–95.

Dresler, M., Shirer, W. R., Konrad, B. N., Müller, N. C. J., Wagner, I. C., Fernández, G., Czisch, M., & Greicius, M. D. (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron, 93(5), 1227–1235.e6.

hops.afterHeading: Wiring the pattern and completing it
hops.title: The magnets behind the Hopfield network
hops.text: Why does a memory model talk about energy? The physicist John Hopfield borrowed the mathematics of magnetic materials, in which each atom's spin makes it a tiny magnet that pushes and pulls on its neighbours. In 1982 he described a network of 30 nodes, all linked by 435 connections, whose stored patterns are meant to sit in energy valleys. Give it a distorted cue and the nodes update one at a time as the energy falls; a cue that starts in the right valley settles into the stored pattern. That work on associative memory was part of what earned Hopfield a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.citation: Hopfield, J. J. (1982). Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities. PNAS, 79(8), 2554–2558; Nobel Prize in Physics 2024 Popular Information.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (2024). Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024.

hops.afterHeading: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation
hops.title: Why playing the answer right after a sleep cue cancels its benefit
hops.text: Many students hope vocabulary played all night will soak in during sleep. The evidence is narrower. Volunteers learned Dutch–German word pairs in the evening, and softly replaying some Dutch words during non-REM sleep improved next-morning recall of the translations; replaying them awake did not. Then the lab played the correct translation right after each cue. That extra sound wiped out the memory boost, and the rise in two sleep rhythms linked to successful cueing, just as a pure tone did. Delay the translation, and the benefit came back. In this experiment, the timing of the sound after the cue made the difference.

sources.citation: Schreiner, T., & Rasch, B. (2015). Boosting vocabulary learning by verbal cueing during sleep. Cerebral Cortex, 25(11), 4169–4179.
Schreiner, T., Lehmann, M., & Rasch, B. (2015). Auditory feedback blocks memory benefits of cueing during sleep. Nature Communications, 6, 8729.

audio.title: Bats in a long tunnel, roses in deep sleep, and the hunt for the Snark
audio.transcript:
Textbook memory research looks tidy: a rat in a small box, a few cells, a clean result. Real brains are messier, and more interesting. Here are three true stories that stretch that picture.

First, take place cells out of the small laboratory box and put them in a very long room. In two thousand twenty-one, researchers in Israel built a flight tunnel two hundred meters long and put tiny wireless recorders on bats flying back and forth inside it. In a small arena, a hippocampal place cell usually fires in one neat patch. In the tunnel, individual neurons in region C A one fired in several patches of very different sizes. Across the neurons, those patches ranged from sixty centimeters to thirty-two meters. Within the same cell, one place field could be twenty times larger than another. Wild-born bats showed this multiscale code from their first day in the tunnel, and bats raised in the lab, which had never experienced a large space, showed it too. A brain mapping the real world does not stick to one zoom level.

Second, what happens to a memory once you fall asleep? In two thousand seven, a team in Germany had volunteers learn the locations of matching card pairs while they breathed the scent of roses. That night, during slow-wave sleep, the researchers quietly piped the same scent back in. The sleepers were not aware of it, yet the next day they remembered more card locations, and brain scans showed the scent activating the hippocampus during slow-wave sleep. Timing was everything. Roses during rapid eye movement sleep, roses while awake, or roses at night when there had been none during learning did nothing. The smell taught nothing new. It appeared to reactivate the hippocampal memory of a game the sleepers already knew.

Finally, if memories are replayed and stored, why has it been so hard to point at one spot and say, there it is? For more than thirty years, Karl Lashley trained rats to run mazes for food, then removed different patches of cortex, trying to erase the maze memory. In those maze tests, the extent of the damage tracked how badly the rats performed better than its location did, though a later reading noted that many of his rats also had unplanned damage to the hippocampus. Lashley joked that the trick was not to find where the trace was located, but where it was not, and in nineteen fifty-seven he compared his quest to Lewis Carroll's poem about hunting a mythical creature called the Snark. In two thousand twenty-two, researchers measured activity in two hundred forty-seven mouse brain regions during fear learning and recall, and flagged one hundred seventeen of them as likely to hold part of the memory trace. Lashley may have been hunting for one drawer when the brain files a single memory across many regions.
